limitations_and_boundaries: Human and murine bile acids have substantially different signaling properties, hampering translational conclusions.
Less abundant or characterized bile acid metabolites may affect interpretation.
Differences in microbiota may explain individual responses to bile acid-derived drugs.
It is not known whether FXR modulation in humans leads to altered microbiota.
It is not known whether TbMCA or GbMCA can antagonize FXR signaling in humans.

research_questions.statement: How do bile acids and gut microbiota interact to influence host metabolism?

provenance.text_excerpt: We have shown that the presence of a gut microbiota reduces the levels of TbMCA, resulting in increased expression of Fgf15 through FXR activation, mainly in the ileum. Thus, we demonstrated that the microbiota regulates both the metabolism and the synthesis of bile acids in an FXR-dependent manner (Sayin et al., 2013).

claims.statement: The gut microbiota regulates bile acid synthesis and FXR signaling by deconjugating TbMCA, an FXR antagonist.

provenance.text_excerpt: a picture emerges that FXR may have beneficial effects on chow diet, whereas on high-fat diet, Fxr-deficiency may protect against metabolic disease, in particular, when intestinal FXR is inhibited.

claims.statement: FXR signaling has context-dependent effects on metabolism: beneficial on chow diet, but FXR deficiency protects against metabolic disease on high-fat diet.

provenance.text_excerpt: It is clear that the microbiota can modulate signaling through both FXR and TGR5 via modifications of bile acids.

claims.statement: Microbiota modulates signaling through both FXR and TGR5 via bile acid modifications.

provenance.text_excerpt: Bile acids can shape the gut microbiota community by promoting the growth of bile acid-metabolizing bacteria and inhibiting the growth of other bile sensitive bacteria.

claims.statement: Bile acids can shape the gut microbiota community by promoting growth of bile acid-metabolizing bacteria and inhibiting bile-sensitive bacteria.

provenance.text_excerpt: Schmitt et al. (2015) observed that hepatic expression of FXR protects against hepatic steatosis and elevated triglyceride and bile acid levels. In contrast, mice with intestinal-specific Fxr deletion were protected against liver steatosis and obesity when fed a high-fat diet (Jiang et al., 2015a; Li et al., 2013). Thus, intestinal and hepatic FXR may have opposing effects on steatosis.

claims.statement: Intestinal and hepatic FXR have opposing effects on steatosis: hepatic FXR protects, while intestinal FXR deletion protects against steatosis on high-fat diet.

evidence_spans.content: FXR activation in colonic L cells inhibits GLP-1 synthesis.

provenance.text_excerpt: In colonic L-cells, FXR activation inhibits the synthesis of GLP-1.

evidence_spans.content: FXR activation in ileum induces FGF15/19, which inhibits CYP7A1 in liver; hepatic FXR induces SHP, also inhibiting CYP7A1.

provenance.text_excerpt: In ileal enterocytes, activation of FXR leads to transcription of FGF15/19, which is secreted into the portal vein and transported to the liver, where it binds to the FGFR4/b-klotho receptor complex on hepatocytes. The FGFR4/b-klotho complex activates JNK/ERK signaling that inhibits expression of CYP7A1. In hepatocytes, binding of bile acids to FXR-RXR heterodimer complex results in transcription of the nuclear receptor SHP, which binds to LRH-1 and thereby also inhibits expression of CYP7A1.

evidence_spans.content: Primary bile acids CDCA and CA activate FXR; LCA and DCA are potent TGR5 ligands; Ta/bMCA and UDCA are FXR antagonists.

provenance.text_excerpt: FXR is activated mainly by the primary bile acids CDCA and CA (labeled in green), while the most potent ligands for TGR5 are LCA and DCA (labeled in blue). Other bile acids, such as Ta/bMCA (primary bile acids in mice) and UDCA, have shown FXR antagonistic properties (labeled in red).

evidence_spans.content: TGR5 activation in colonic L cells increases GLP-1 synthesis; in skeletal muscle and brown adipose tissue increases energy expenditure via thyroid hormone conversion.

provenance.text_excerpt: TGR5 activation in colonic L cells increases synthesis and release of GLP-1. TGR5 in skeletal muscle and brown adipose tissue increases energy expenditure by promoting the conversion of inactive thyroxine (T4) into active thyroid hormone (T3).

experiments_or_tasks: Investigation of gut microbiota regulation of bile acid synthesis enzymes (CYP7A1, CYP7B1, CYP27A1) and FXR signaling.

methods.name: Germ-free mouse model
methods.protocol_description: Comparison of germ-free (GF) mice with colonized mice to study microbial effects on bile acid metabolism and FXR signaling.

study_units.name: Microbial regulation of bile acid synthesis and signaling

results.metric_name: Bariatric surgery effects on microbiota and bile acids

results.value_raw_text: Bariatric surgery alters gut microbiota composition; RYGB patients show increased postprandial bile acid and FGF19 response.

results.metric_name: Tempol effect on microbiota and FXR

provenance.text_excerpt: they observed that Tempol decreased the genera Lactobacillus and Clostridium (clusters IV and XIV), which was accompanied by decreased BSH activity and accumulation of intestinal TbMCA.

results.value_raw_text: Tempol decreased Lactobacillus and Clostridium, reduced BSH activity, and increased TbMCA, suppressing FXR signaling.

provenance.text_excerpt: Treatment with OCA for 6 weeks in patients with NAFLD and T2DM dose-dependently improved insulin sensitivity, estimated by euglycemic clamp, and reduced body weight, compared with placebo (Mudaliar et al., 2013). A multicenter, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled, phase 3a study with OCA (FLINT) in 283 patients with NASH, with and without T2DM, demonstrated that 72 weeks of treatment with OCA led to significant improvement in the NAS (NASH activity score). Improvement of fibrosis was also observed in the OCA treatment group compared with controls (Neuschwander-Tetri et al., 2015).

results.value_raw_text: OCA treatment for 6 weeks in NAFLD and T2DM patients improved insulin sensitivity and reduced body weight; 72-week OCA treatment improved NAS and fibrosis.

provenance.text_excerpt: Schmitt et al. (2015) observed that hepatic expression of FXR protects against hepatic steatosis and elevated triglyceride and bile acid levels. results.value_raw_text: Hepatic FXR protects against steatosis; intestinal FXR deletion protects against steatosis and obesity on high-fat diet.

provenance.text_excerpt: experiments with Tgr5-deficient mice showed that TGR5 did not contribute to the reduced body weight, increased energy expenditure, or increased glucose-stimulated insulin secretion after vertical sleeve gastrectomy (VSG) (McGavigan et al., 2015). However, glucose tolerance, hepatic insulin signaling, and metabolically favorable changes in bile acid profiles after VSG were attenuated in the Tgr5-deficient mice, indicating that TGR5 has an impact on at least some of the beneficial effects after bariatric surgery.

results.value_raw_text: TGR5 does not contribute to reduced body weight or energy expenditure after VSG, but affects glucose tolerance and bile acid profiles.

results.value_raw_text: CDCA increased BAT activity and energy expenditure in humans; LCA and TGR5 agonists had similar effects.
